n: The people of Judah made sixteen-year-old Uzziah king after his father Amaziah.

f.g: Also called Azariah in Kings; both names mean roughly ‘the LORD is my strength/help.’

n: He rebuilt Eloth (Elath), the Red Sea port, and returned it to Judah, reopening trade routes.

f.g: Elath, on the Gulf of Aqaba.

n: Uzziah reigned fifty-two years (about 792–740 BC, including years co-reigning) — one of Judah’s longest reigns. His mother was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.
He did right in the Lord’s sight, as his father had in his better years.
He sought God during the lifetime of Zechariah, a teacher who understood the visions (or ‘fear’) of God. As long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper — the key verse of his life.

f.g: A spiritual adviser otherwise unknown; not the later prophet.

f.w: as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper

n: He fought the Philistines, broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod, and built towns in Philistine territory.

f.g: One of the five main Philistine cities.

n: God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabs of Gur-baal, and the Meunites.

f.g: Meunites, a people of the Arabian or Edomite region.

n: The Ammonites paid him tribute, and his fame reached Egypt’s border because he became very powerful.
Uzziah built and fortified towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the Angle — partly repairing damage from his father’s defeat.

f.g: The angle or bend in the wall.

n: He built towers and dug wells in the wilderness for his herds, and employed farmers and vinedressers, for he loved the soil. A king who cared for agriculture strengthened his people’s livelihood.

f.g: Here probably meaning fertile land or orchards, not necessarily Mount Carmel.

n: He had a well-organized army, mustered by divisions under the scribe Jeiel and the official Maaseiah, supervised by Hananiah.
The army had 2,600 family heads as officers.
Under them were 307,500 trained soldiers ready to defend the king.
Uzziah equipped his whole army with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingstones — unusual, since soldiers often had to supply their own gear.
He built inventive devices on Jerusalem’s towers to shoot arrows and hurl large stones. His fame spread, for he was marvelously helped — until he became strong.

f.g: Machines of war — perhaps defensive frameworks or early catapults.
A warning phrase: help from God until strength led to pride.

n: But strength led to pride. Uzziah entered the temple to burn incense on the incense altar — a sacred duty given only to priests.

f.w: his heart was lifted up to his destruction

n: Azariah the high priest followed him in with eighty courageous priests to stop him.

f.g: Brave men — it took courage to confront the king.

n: They confronted the king: burning incense isn’t your right, Uzziah, but belongs to Aaron’s consecrated descendants. Leave the sanctuary — you have sinned. Priesthood authority cannot be taken, only given by God.

f.g: It does not belong to you.

n: Uzziah, censer in hand, raged at the priests — and right then leprosy broke out on his forehead beside the incense altar.

f.g: A term for various serious skin diseases that made one ritually unclean.

n: Seeing the leprosy on his forehead, the priests hurried him out — and he hurried to leave, for the Lord had struck him.

Uzziah remained leprous until death, living in isolation and barred from the temple. His son Jotham governed in his place. The king who reached for priestly power lost even ordinary access to God’s house.
Isaiah the prophet wrote the rest of Uzziah’s history. Isaiah’s great vision of the Lord came “in the year that king Uzziah died.”

f.w: Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz

n: Uzziah was buried in a field next to the royal tombs, not in them, because he was a leper. Jotham became king.
